title: Sparsity-aware fusedops profiling diary
content:
Purpose:
Quick field diary for experiments comparing sparsity-aware fused ops vs vanilla fusedops vs FlashPaged implementations for attention kernels. Goal: surface case(s) where exploiting structured sparsity (patterned token pruning) leads to net latency win under our runtime constraints (small/medium batches, tail SLOs).

Context / motivation:
- We've seen interest from several customers for lower-cost inference on instruction-heavy prompts where many tokens are padding-ish or repeated (chat histories).
- Prior notes focused on fusion and prefetching; fewer experiments touched on sparsity integrated into fused kernels (i.e., skip-work paths that avoid loading QKV for pruned token positions).
- Hypothesis: a sparsity-aware fused op can reduce DRAM/TensorCore bandwidth and kernel time, but only if (a) the sparsity is structured (block or run-length) and (b) kernel launch/queue overhead doesn't dominate for small batch sizes.

Hardware / software baseline:
- GPUs: NVIDIA A100 40GB (prod), NVIDIA H100 80GB (dev cluster).
- CUDA toolkit: 12.2 on H100, 11.7 on A100 (matching runtime builds).
- Runtime: serving-runtime branch sparsity-experiments (PR linked above).
- Models: 7B architecture shim (Llama-like), single-layer attention microbench harness extracted from the runtime to avoid whole-model noise.
- Tools: nvprof replaced by Nsight Systems collect (sys profile), nvtx ranges emitted from microbench harness, torch.profiler used for CPU/GPU timings.

Experiment matrix (high level):
- Implementations: (1) FlashAttention optimized (flashpaged fallback enabled), (2) Vanilla fused ops (current fused kernels), (3) Sparsity-aware fused ops (new branch implementing block-run skip).
- Sparsity types: none (dense), structured-block (every 4 tokens pruned), run-length (random runs, avg 30% tokens pruned), random-sparse (unstructured ~30%).
- Batch sizes: B=1,2,4,8
- Seq lengths: L=64,128,512
- Quantization: FP16 baseline; INT8 experiments later (not in this diary).

Representative run command (harness):
python microbench_attention.py --impl=sparse-fused --batch=2 --seq=128 --sparsity=block4 --device=a100 --repeat=200 --nvtx

Key observations (initial runs):
1) Dense case: flashoptimized wins at larger seq lengths (512) and B>=4. For small sequences (64) and B<=2 the launch + prefetch costs for FlashPaged make it comparable or slightly worse than fusedops.
2) Structured-block sparsity (block4): sparsity-aware fusedops shows ~20-28% kernel time reduction at L=128/B=2 on A100. Actual end-to-end tail latency (p95) improved by ~12% because scheduler queuing increased slightly (more small kernels).
3) Run-length sparsity (random runs): benefits vary — when average contiguous run length >8 tokens we see good locality gains (~15%). If runs are short and numerous, overhead of branch logic erodes gains.
4) Unstructured random sparsity: no wins — memory access patterns cause thread divergence and TensorCore underutilization.
5) H100 shows greater sensitivity to launch overheads; fusedop wins are smaller on H100 for dense large batches where FlashAttention kernel autotuning is aggressive. H100 benefit for sparse fusedops appears slightly larger relative to A100 (maybe due to better scheduling), but absolute latency still depends on seq/batch shape.

Micro-metrics (sample numbers, A100, FP16, mean of 200 iters):
- Dense, L=128, B=2:
  FlashPaged: avg kernel time 6.2 ms, p95 9.1 ms, throughput tokens/s 34k
  FusedOps: avg kernel time 6.9 ms, p95 9.6 ms, throughput tokens/s 31k
  SparseFused (0% sparsity control): avg 6.8 ms (sanity check)

- Block4 sparsity (~25% tokens removed), L=128, B=2:
  FlashPaged: avg kernel time 5.9 ms (no special handling), p95 8.8 ms
  FusedOps: avg kernel time 5.5 ms, p95 7.2 ms
  SparseFused: avg kernel time 4.2 ms, p95 5.1 ms, throughput tokens/s 38.6k (note: tokens denominator excludes pruned tokens)

- Run-length sparsity (avg run length 12, 30% removal), L=512, B=4:
  SparseFused: avg kernel time 12.1 ms (win vs fusedops 14.3 ms), but we saw larger variance due to queueing and occasional re-warmups.

Profiling notes / flame graph signals:
- Nsight capture with NVTX: sparse fused kernel reduces memory load time (ld.global) and L2 bandwidth by ~25% in block cases. Effective achieved occupancy dropped slightly (~2-5%) but FP throughput utilization stayed high.
- Host-side: more frequent small kernel launches; driver overhead accounted for ~5-8% of total per-request latency in best-case sparse runs, up to ~20% in tiny batch/seq configurations.
- Kernel name mapping: sparse-fused kernel has a short latency-critical code path and a fallback path that reuses the vanilla fused kernel when pattern mismatch detected. We need to ensure fallback counts are logged — some runs unexpectedly triggered fallback due to alignment differences in padded buffers.

Gotchas and surprises:
- Alignment sensitivity: our sparse fused kernel assumes contiguous memory for blocks. If upstream pre-padding doesn't align on 128-byte stride we see fallback or mispredictions. Runtime should either realign buffers or add a small memcopy fast-path.
- NVTX ranges show many small kernels emitted from the scheduler for sparse runs (one kernel per active token block). On busy machines this increases latency variance. Solutions: coalesce blocks into batches when possible or do host-side aggregation to create larger kernels.
- FlashPaged + sparsity: FlashPaged currently treats pruned tokens as zeroed, which reduces work but still pays for data movement. Integrating a genuine skip path into FlashPaged is nontrivial because it relies on contiguous KV cache indexing.
- Memory footprint: SparseFused sometimes reduces peak GPU memory (KV storage) by ~10% which helps multi-model consolidation. But bookkeeping arrays (bitmasks, index maps) add overhead for high token counts; net memory saved depends on sparsity fraction and scale.

Small experiment: sparse coalescing heuristic
- Implemented naive coalescer that combines adjacent sparse blocks up to a target block size 32.
- Result: reduced number of launches by ~40% and improved p95 by ~15% for L=512/B=4 runs. Tradeoff: added extra copy to build coalesced buffer (~0.4 ms overhead) which pays off at larger seqs.

Operational metrics to capture (we'll integrate into Console):
- fraction_of_requests_with_sparsity (per-route): to estimate benefit potential
- sparse_fused_fallback_rate: % of calls where sparse kernel fell back to vanilla
- avg_kernel_launches_per_request: helps detect driver overhead inflation
- bytes_saved_by_sparsity: L2/DRAM delta per-request

Next experiments (planned):
1) INT8 path: measure whether quantization reduces divergence overhead or amplifies it (suspect amplification).
2) Kernel coalescer refinement: attempt zero-copy coalescing using page-aligned buffer pools rather than per-request memcopy.
3) FlashPaged rewrite exploration: prototype a skip-index layer that maps active token indices to compact KV slices and reuse existing FlashAttention inner loops. Risky but high payoff for large-batch chat workloads.
4) Scheduler-level batching: let scheduler aggregate multiple small sparse requests (same model/version) within microtime windows to create higher effective B and amortize launch overhead.

Notes to reviewers / TODOs:
- Arjun: please add fallback logging hooks in PR 783 so we can get precise fallback counts per test run.
- Lena: can you run the run-length experiments with different RNG seeds and collect histograms of run length distribution? I saw some runs dominated by many tiny runs which killed benefits.
- Maya (me): isolate buffer alignment cases and add automated repro that triggers fallback deterministically.

Raw trace artifacts saved in experiment bucket: gs://rinf-perf/sparsity-experiments/2024-11-12/ (nsys.qdrep, nvtx.json, perf.csv) — link ephemeral until pinned in Confluence.

Preliminary conclusions (working):
- Structured sparsity is helpful when pattern granularity is coarse (block sizes >=4 and contiguous runs).
- Wins are controlled by kernel launch overhead and coalescing ability; runtime-level aggregation/scheduler changes are as important as kernel-level codegen.
- FlashPaged remains the best option for dense heavy workloads; sparse fused ops are a complementary optimization for chat-like workloads with meaningful token pruning.

This doc will evolve as we add INT8/quant paths and scheduler batching trials. Keep notes messy — this is a lab diary rather than a polished writeup.

References and quick links:
- Slack thread: #perf-fusedops sparse experiments (link: slack://channels/C12345)
- PR: https://github.com/redwood-inference/serving-runtime/pull/783 (sparse-fusedops initial impl)
- JIRA: RINF-2345 (customer ask: "lower cost for chat with repeated system messages")

End of diary entry.
